paragraphs: Generating several reasoning paths can improve a language model’s answers, but it also raises a selection problem: how should those paths determine confidence in an answer? This paper develops a theoretical framework around confidence estimation to analyze sampling-based test-time scaling. It examines self-consistency, which uses agreement among outputs, and perplexity, which uses the model’s internal probabilities.

The analysis separates estimation error from modeling error. Self-consistency has high estimation error, while perplexity introduces substantial modeling error and can worsen how estimation error converges. The proposed RPC method combines the two through Perplexity Consistency and removes low-probability reasoning paths through Reasoning Pruning. Within the framework, the combination improves estimation-error convergence from linear to exponential while preserving modeling error.

Theory and experiments across seven benchmarks support RPC’s potential to reduce reasoning error. Empirically, it matches self-consistency’s reasoning performance while improving confidence reliability and cutting sampling costs by 50%. The contribution connects more reliable answer selection with using fewer sampled reasoning paths.
neurips-2025-a-theoretical-study-on-brid.tldr: RPC combines answer agreement, internal probabilities, and reasoning pruning to improve confidence reliability while matching self-consistency with 50% lower sampling costs.

paragraphs: Counterfactual analysis asks how an outcome would change if an agent acted differently. For language model agents, defining that alternative action is difficult because actions are expressed through open-ended text. Changing individual tokens may fail to capture the behavioral difference a user cares about, and a token’s meaning can change with its surrounding context.

Abstract Counterfactuals moves the focus to higher-level properties of actions and interactions with an environment. This lets the counterfactual question be framed around user-relevant features instead of depending entirely on particular words. The approach addresses a central mismatch between the textual form of an agent’s output and the action that output represents.

The authors test the framework in text-based games and counterfactual text generation, considering interventions at both token and latent-space levels. They report consistent, meaningful counterfactuals with fewer unwanted side effects than token-level methods. These findings support abstraction as a useful way to evaluate alternative agent behavior while reducing changes unrelated to the intended question.
neurips-2025-abstract-counterfactuals-fo.tldr: Abstract Counterfactuals evaluates alternative language-agent behavior through high-level action properties, producing meaningful counterfactuals with fewer unwanted token-level side effects.

paragraphs: Reinforcement fine-tuning can spend substantial effort revisiting the same queries under uniform sampling. This paper asks whether a model’s own internal activity can identify data it is better positioned to learn from. Its proposed signal, angle concentration, describes the angular distribution of the hidden-state vectors associated with tokens.

The authors establish a theoretical and empirical correlation between that distribution and the resulting training gradient. Their findings indicate a learning preference for examples with higher angle concentration. GAIN-RL uses this signal to select training data dynamically during each epoch, connecting data selection to the model’s current learning behavior instead of relying only on a heuristic measure of difficulty.

Across the reported mathematical and coding tasks and model scales, GAIN-RL with GRPO achieves more than a 2.5-fold improvement in training efficiency. It also obtains better performance using half the original training data than standard GRPO using the full dataset. These results support internal representation geometry as a useful signal for allocating reinforcement-training effort.
neurips-2025-angles-dont-lie-unlocking-t.tldr: GAIN-RL selects training examples using hidden-state angle concentration, improving reported GRPO training efficiency by over 2.5 times.

paragraphs: Quaternions offer geometric advantages for representing rotations and postures, motivating this supervised neural network built around quaternion-valued neurons. The model extends a fully connected, continuous-time Hopfield formulation into quaternion algebra. The authors establish the existence and uniqueness of fixed points with asymptotic stability, giving the network’s evolving state a mathematical foundation for settling toward a stable solution.

Training uses gradient descent together with periodic projection. At regular intervals, each four-by-four block of the weight matrix is projected onto the nearest quaternion-compatible structure in a least-squares sense. This provides a concrete way to maintain the required algebraic organization while preserving convergence during learning.

Experiments on randomly generated target sets report high accuracy, fast convergence, and reliability. The network’s trajectories also have bounded curvature, supporting the smooth evolution relevant to robotic posture control and path planning. Those applications motivate the design; the stated experimental evidence concerns target sets. More broadly, the work offers a method for constructing networks whose learning rules respect hypercomplex algebraic structure.
neurips-2025-asymptotically-stable-quate.tldr: A quaternion-valued Hopfield network combines stable dynamics with periodic weight projection to preserve quaternion structure during supervised learning.

paragraphs: Automatic rigging must produce a connected skeleton and determine how that skeleton influences a model’s surface. Auto-Connect builds skeletal connectivity directly into the sequence it predicts. Special tokens mark the endpoints of each joint’s children and each hierarchical layer, allowing the generated representation to express how joints belong together.

This representation addresses topology alongside joint placement. The method then uses a reward that measures topological correctness to guide a post-training phase with Direct Preference Optimization. Connectivity-aware prediction and reward-guided refinement therefore target the structure of the skeleton at two stages of the process.

For skinning, which assigns bone influence to surface vertices, Auto-Connect incorporates implicit geodesic features into latent top-k bone selection. Distance information in the latent space helps select the most influential bones for each vertex and reduces common skinning artifacts. The authors report more anatomically plausible skeletal structures and better deformation properties from the combined method. Its contribution spans both constructing the skeletal hierarchy and connecting that hierarchy to surface movement.
neurips-2025-auto-connect-connectivity-p.tldr: Auto-Connect integrates skeletal connectivity, topology-guided preference optimization, and geodesic-aware bone selection to improve automatic rigging and deformation.

paragraphs: This paper studies whether language models can infer the consequences of hypothetical changes from information supplied in context. It begins with a synthetic linear regression task where success requires recovering an unseen latent concept and carrying over the contextual noise from factual observations. That second requirement, noise abduction, makes the task specifically counterfactual.

The authors show that language models can perform this task and strengthen theoretical identifiability results. For a broad class of functions, they reduce counterfactual reasoning to a transformation of the observations supplied in context. In Transformers, their analysis identifies self-attention, depth, and diversity of pretraining data as drivers of performance.

Mechanistic evidence indicates that the latent concept has a linear representation in the residual stream. The authors also identify attention heads central to noise abduction. Results extend to sequential data governed by stochastic differential equations, showing that Transformers can recover relevant noise in that setting. The suggested connection to counterfactual story generation remains preliminary, grounded in these controlled and sequential reasoning findings.
neurips-2025-counterfactual-reasoning-an.tldr: Controlled tasks show Transformers can perform in-context counterfactual reasoning by recovering latent concepts and carrying factual noise into hypothetical predictions.

paragraphs: EEG patterns vary in both duration and spatial extent: some are brief and localized, while others involve slower rhythms or distributed brain regions. CSBrain is built around this diversity. The paper argues that dense modeling approaches which ignore scale can produce weaker representations for decoding different kinds of brain activity.

Its first component, Cross-scale Spatiotemporal Tokenization, combines features at several scales within local time windows and anatomical regions. This produces compact tokens that retain scale information. Structured Sparse Attention then models dependencies across those windows and regions while removing spurious dependencies. Alternating the two components progressively integrates information across spatial and temporal scales.

Across 11 EEG tasks and 16 datasets, CSBrain consistently outperforms the evaluated task-specific models and strong foundation-model baselines. The findings support cross-scale structure as a useful architectural bias for generalized EEG decoding. The significance is that the model organizes its representations around the varied spatial and temporal patterns in neural activity, and this design transfers across the tested tasks.
neurips-2025-csbrain-a-cross-scale-spati.tldr: CSBrain models EEG activity across spatial and temporal scales, consistently outperforming evaluated baselines across 11 tasks and 16 datasets.

paragraphs: A correct diagnostic answer does not reveal whether a vision-language model can connect medical knowledge to the anatomy visible in an X-ray. This work introduces CheXStruct and CXReasonBench to evaluate that connection through intermediate steps. Both are built on the publicly available MIMIC-CXR-JPG dataset.

CheXStruct automatically derives a structured sequence from chest images: anatomical segmentation, landmarks and measurements, diagnostic indices, and application of clinical thresholds. CXReasonBench uses this pipeline to test whether models can carry out clinically meaningful steps and learn from structured guidance. Its evaluations include selecting anatomical regions and making diagnostic measurements across multiple stages and reasoning paths.

The benchmark contains 18,988 question-answer pairs covering 12 diagnostic tasks and 1,200 cases, with up to four visual inputs per case. All 12 evaluated models, including the strongest, struggle with structured reasoning and generalization. Their difficulty linking abstract knowledge to anatomically grounded interpretation shows why assessing intermediate reasoning provides information that final-answer evaluation alone can miss.
neurips-2025-cxreasonbench-a-benchmark-f.tldr: CXReasonBench evaluates anatomical and measurement-based reasoning in chest X-rays, exposing difficulties even in the strongest of 12 tested vision-language models.

paragraphs: Vision Transformers commonly divide images into fixed patches before processing them. Those divisions do not adapt to the spatial or semantic structure of the image. This paper introduces a visual tokenizer that responds to image content at pixel-level granularity, making the formation of tokens itself an adaptive part of the model.

The tokenizer is differentiable from end to end, allowing it to participate in the same learning process as the surrounding architecture. It uses hierarchical model selection guided by information criteria to organize the image representation. Backward compatibility with existing architectures is a central feature: the method can be used to retrofit pretrained models.

The authors report competitive performance for both image-level classification and dense prediction, where outputs concern locations throughout an image. They also report raster-to-vector conversion without additional adaptation. Together, these capabilities show that content-adaptive tokenization can support different output requirements while retaining compatibility with established Vision Transformer designs. The stated performance claim is competitiveness across these tasks.
neurips-2025-differentiable-hierarchical.tldr: A differentiable, hierarchical tokenizer adapts visual tokens to image content while supporting pretrained architectures, competitive prediction, and raster-to-vector conversion.

paragraphs: Some statistical models are easy to simulate but have likelihood functions that cannot be evaluated tractably. This makes direct likelihood maximization difficult. The paper proposes estimating the Fisher score, the quantity that supplies a direction for improving the likelihood, and using that estimate in a sequential gradient-based optimization procedure.

At each parameter iterate, the method simulates from a localized surrounding region and applies local score matching. A linear parameterization of the surrogate score model makes fitting it a closed-form least-squares problem. The resulting score approximation effectively smooths the likelihood objective, helping the optimization navigate complex likelihood landscapes.

The authors provide theoretical guarantees for the estimator, including bounds on the bias that smoothing introduces. This explicitly connects the method’s stabilizing effect to the approximation error it creates. Experiments on synthetic and real-world problems report better performance than the evaluated benchmarks. The approach is therefore supported by both analysis of its score estimates and evidence that those estimates are useful for optimization when simulations are available.
neurips-2025-direct-fisher-score-estimat.tldr: Local simulations and a closed-form score estimator enable gradient-based likelihood maximization when likelihood evaluation is intractable.

paragraphs: Diffusion models generate images through repeated denoising, which makes sampling slow but exposes intermediate states that can be inspected or edited. Direct one-step mappings accelerate generation while sacrificing access to that process. Hierarchical Koopman Diffusion aims to retain an interpretable trajectory while producing samples in one step.

The method maps nonlinear diffusion dynamics into a latent space governed by globally linear operators. In that representation, trajectories have closed-form solutions, eliminating the need to simulate each denoising step in sequence. Intermediate states remain accessible, so a user can still intervene during generation. A hierarchical architecture separates dynamics across spatial resolutions using scale-specific Koopman subspaces.

This hierarchy captures image development from coarse structure to finer detail. Experiments report competitive one-step generation performance, together with a mechanism for analyzing and manipulating the generative process through spectral analysis. The contribution is a formulation in which fast endpoint generation and access to the path toward that endpoint coexist, preserving a form of control that direct noise-to-image mappings can lose.
neurips-2025-hierarchical-koopman-diffus.tldr: Hierarchical Koopman Diffusion uses linear latent dynamics for one-step image generation while retaining interpretable, editable intermediate states.

paragraphs: Data valuation assigns training examples scores that can guide cleaning, acquisition, or selection. Existing methods may inherit the biases of a fitted model or require many expensive training runs. KAIROS instead measures each example’s contribution to the discrepancy between the training data and a clean reference distribution, without depending on a particular fitted model.

Its discrepancy measure is Maximum Mean Discrepancy, or MMD. The authors use a closed-form solution that avoids the approximations needed by competing Wasserstein-based approaches. The framework also supports incremental updates: adding a batch of m examples requires O(mN) computation to update all scores, compared with O(N²) in the cited prior approach, where N is the training-set size.

On noise, mislabeling, and poisoning benchmarks, KAIROS consistently improves accuracy and runtime over the evaluated state-of-the-art baselines. On ImageNet, it is up to 15 times faster than the fastest baseline while retaining better valuation quality. These results support scalable valuation without a fitted model, using a clean reference distribution as the basis for judging examples.
neurips-2025-kairos-scalable-model-agnos.tldr: KAIROS values training examples through MMD against a clean reference distribution, improving reported valuation quality and achieving up to 15-fold speedup.

paragraphs: Constructive neural routing methods build solutions incrementally, often by appending each newly chosen location to a partial route. That construction rule limits the choices available at each step. L2C-Insert expands the action space by allowing an unvisited location to be inserted at any valid position in the current partial solution.

The framework includes an architecture designed to predict insertion positions, an efficient training scheme, and an inference technique that exploits the flexibility of insertion. These components make choosing where a location belongs part of the learned construction process. The approach therefore changes how a solution is assembled, giving each new location more possible placements as construction proceeds.

Experiments cover synthetic and real-world instances of the Travelling Salesman Problem and Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem across multiple sizes. The authors report consistently superior performance in these evaluations. The findings support insertion as a useful design choice for neural combinatorial optimization: a more flexible construction operation can improve solution quality when paired with appropriate prediction, training, and inference methods.
neurips-2025-learning-to-insert-for-cons.tldr: L2C-Insert learns to place unvisited locations anywhere valid in partial routes, improving reported routing performance across problem sizes.

paragraphs: High-resolution images make Vision Transformers expensive because the number of image tokens grows rapidly with resolution. LookWhere learns where to spend computation before fully processing the high-resolution input. It divides work between a low-resolution selector and a high-resolution extractor, so detailed processing is directed toward selected image content.

The two components are pretrained jointly by distilling a self-supervised teacher, without task supervision. This teaches both selection and representation extraction in the same process. It also avoids paying the initial processing cost of tokens that would later be pruned. The resulting image representations transfer to recognition tasks without the complex per-task selection optimization described for prior methods.

On high-resolution Traffic Signs recognition, LookWhere maintains accuracy while reducing floating-point operations by a factor of 17 and time by a factor of four. For ImageNet classification and ADE20K segmentation, the authors report improved accuracy and a 1.36-fold time reduction. The results cover both global image understanding and local prediction, supporting learned selection as a practical source of computational savings.
neurips-2025-lookwhere-efficient-visual-.tldr: LookWhere jointly learns low-resolution selection and high-resolution feature extraction, reducing recognition costs while maintaining or improving reported accuracy.

paragraphs: MGE-LDM brings music creation and source extraction into one latent diffusion framework. It learns a joint distribution over complete musical mixtures, mixtures containing only some sources, and individual source tracks, or stems. This shared representation supports working with music at several levels of composition within a single compact model.

At inference, the model can generate a complete mixture, generate missing sources, or extract a source described through text. Separation and source imputation are both formulated as conditional inpainting in latent space. In this formulation, the available information conditions the process of producing the requested source content.

The framework does not depend on a predefined list of instrument categories. That design supports class-agnostic manipulation and joint training across heterogeneous multitrack datasets, including Slakh2100, MUSDB18, and MoisesDB. The contribution described in the abstract is this unified capability: generation, completion, and extraction share one model and one conditional formulation. It provides a way to accommodate differently organized music datasets without requiring a common fixed instrument taxonomy.
neurips-2025-mge-ldm-joint-latent-diffus.tldr: MGE-LDM unifies music generation, missing-source generation, and text-guided source extraction through conditional inpainting in a shared latent diffusion model.

paragraphs: Variational inference approximates a Bayesian posterior with a tractable distribution, but complex hierarchical models can produce geometry that is difficult to capture. This paper connects two approaches to that problem: flow-based variational families and Variationally Inferred Parameters, or VIP. Its starting point is a formal relationship between their representations.

The authors prove that VIP combined with a full-rank Gaussian can be represented exactly by a forward autoregressive flow when that flow includes a translation term and information from the model’s prior. This is an exact equivalence for the specified combination. It identifies concrete ingredients that a flow needs to express that construction.

The proposed Model-Informed Flow architecture incorporates those ingredients: translation, prior information, and hierarchical ordering. Experiments on hierarchical and non-hierarchical benchmarks show tighter posterior approximations and performance matching or exceeding the evaluated state of the art. The work uses a theoretical connection to guide architecture design, showing how information already present in the Bayesian model can help shape a more effective approximation.
neurips-2025-model-informed-flows-for-ba.tldr: Model-Informed Flows incorporate prior information, translation, and hierarchical ordering to improve Bayesian posterior approximation.

paragraphs: Predictive coding is a brain-inspired learning approach that uses local information, but training very deep predictive coding networks has been difficult. This paper analyzes how their behavior changes with scale and identifies several instabilities that emerge at large depths. It introduces μPC, a Depth-μP parameterization intended to make that scaling more reliable.

The method addresses only some of the identified instabilities, yet enables stable training of residual networks with up to 128 layers. On simple classification tasks, these networks achieve competitive performance with little tuning relative to current benchmarks. The result establishes that predictive coding can train substantially deeper networks under the studied setup.

μPC also permits weight and activity learning rates to transfer across network widths and depths without retuning for the new size. That matters because optimization settings can otherwise make scaling experiments costly and fragile. The authors frame the work as a first step toward more complex architectures, with possible implications for other local learning algorithms. The demonstrated scope remains deep residual networks on simple classification tasks.
neurips-2025-mu-pc-scaling-predictive-co.tldr: μPC enables stable predictive-coding training of residual networks up to 128 layers on simple classification tasks and transfers learning rates across sizes.

paragraphs: Agents can extend their perception by sharing intermediate features, but those features may be incompatible when agents use different fixed models. Existing alignment methods often choose one agent’s representation as the shared target. Agents whose features differ greatly from that target can then be difficult to align.

NegoCollab learns a common representation through negotiation among local representations during training. Paired sender and receiver components transform features between each agent’s local space and the common space. This gives the shared representation input from the participating modalities instead of assigning one agent’s feature space as the reference for everyone.

Training combines distribution alignment with structural and pragmatic alignment losses to distill knowledge from the common representation into the senders. The authors report substantial improvements over existing methods based on common representations. The findings support negotiating the shared feature space as a useful way to reduce discrepancies among heterogeneous agents. The contribution is especially relevant to the stated setting where the participating perception models are different and remain fixed.
neurips-2025-negocollab-a-common-represe.tldr: NegoCollab negotiates a shared feature representation among agents with different fixed perception models, improving reported collaborative perception performance.

paragraphs: Automated machine learning must decide both which model class to use and how to tune its hyperparameters. These decisions compete for resources: effort spent exploring another class cannot simultaneously refine a promising existing choice. This paper treats that combined selection and tuning problem as a resource allocation task.

The proposed MaxUCB method uses a max k-armed bandit formulation to balance exploration across model classes with hyperparameter optimization. Its design targets bounded and light-tailed reward distributions, the types the authors identify in this setting. That distributional choice matters because classic max-bandit approaches assuming heavy-tailed rewards are a less suitable basis for this particular allocation problem.

The authors evaluate MaxUCB theoretically and empirically, including experiments on four standard AutoML benchmarks. They report superior performance over prior approaches and present it as an efficient alternative to classic max-bandit methods. The contribution links the statistical properties of the rewards to the allocation strategy, supporting a method specifically designed for finding strong model configurations within the combined search.
neurips-2025-put-cash-on-bandits-a-max-k.tldr: MaxUCB allocates AutoML effort between model-class exploration and hyperparameter tuning using a max-bandit method designed for bounded, light-tailed rewards.

paragraphs: Virtual environments need sound that changes appropriately as a source moves. This paper introduces resounding: estimating a room’s impulse responses for arbitrary emitter locations from measurements at only a sparse set of emitter positions. An impulse response characterizes how sound travels through the room, making it useful for reproducing spatial audio.

Versa uses acoustic reciprocity to expand the available training information. By exchanging emitter and listener poses, it creates physically valid samples with dense virtual emitter positions. This turns a physical property of sound propagation into a mechanism for learning the acoustic field from limited measured source locations.

Applying reciprocity is complicated by emitter and listener gain patterns, and the authors introduce a self-supervised approach to handle that challenge. On simulated and real-world datasets, Versa substantially improves acoustic-field learning across the evaluated metrics. Perceptual user studies also report better immersive spatial sound. These findings connect the additional physically grounded samples to both model performance and the experience of listening in a virtual environment.
neurips-2025-resounding-acoustic-fields-.tldr: Versa uses acoustic reciprocity to create virtual emitter samples from sparse measurements, improving acoustic-field learning and perceived spatial sound.

paragraphs: Logical constraints can encourage an autonomous-driving detector to produce predictions consistent with common-sense rules. To train with those rules, violations must be translated into a numerical loss. T-norms provide that translation, and this paper studies how their selection affects the detector’s behavior.

MOD-ECL implements a broad range of t-norms and selects well-performing choices during training. A separate scheduler controls how much the constraint loss influences learning. These two mechanisms allow the framework to adapt both the form of the logical penalty and its strength, addressing the risk that a poorly chosen fixed formulation produces unwanted behavior.

Experiments on ROAD-R and ROAD-Waymo-R use the datasets’ attached common-sense constraints. The results show that parameter selection is crucial for making constrained losses behave effectively. MOD-ECL reduces rule violations and sometimes also improves detection performance. Its contribution includes finer control over the trade-off between accuracy and constraint compliance; the reported accuracy improvements apply to some cases, while improved compliance is the broader stated outcome.
neurips-2025-t-norm-selection-for-object.tldr: MOD-ECL adaptively selects logical-loss formulations and their training influence to reduce constraint violations, with detection improvements in some cases.

paragraphs: Extra computation during diffusion sampling can improve generated outputs, but simply adding denoising steps quickly gives diminishing returns. This paper instead searches over the sequence of injected noise vectors. Those choices influence the final sample, creating another way to spend inference-time computation toward a desired reward.

The authors first formulate diffusion as a Markov Decision Process with a terminal reward. This makes tree search conceptually appropriate but computationally impractical. They then relax the problem into a sequence of independent contextual bandits. Their epsilon-greedy algorithm explores broadly at extreme timesteps and exploits locally during intermediate steps, where de-mixing occurs.

Experiments with EDM and Stable Diffusion report state-of-the-art scores for class-conditioned and text-to-image generation, improvements over baselines of up to 164%, and performance matching or exceeding Monte Carlo tree search. The method supports rewards that need not be differentiable. The contribution is a practical search strategy for the whole noise trajectory, using a simplified decision formulation to balance quality with the expense of evaluating candidate trajectories.
neurips-2025-test-time-scaling-of-diffus.tldr: A contextual-bandit search optimizes diffusion noise trajectories at inference time, improving reported generation scores while supporting non-differentiable rewards.

paragraphs: The Matrix is a world simulator that generates realistic video while responding to movement controls in first- or third-person views. The authors describe a capacity for indefinitely long 720p streams and report continuous, uncut sequences lasting an hour. At speeds of up to 16 frames per second, the system supports interactive traversal through varied environments.

Training combines limited supervised video-game data with large amounts of unsupervised real-world footage. The game data includes Forza Horizon 5 and Cyberpunk 2077, while the real footage includes settings such as Tokyo streets. This combination is intended to transfer controllable movement learned from games into realistic contexts where collecting continuous movement data is difficult.

The reported zero-shot generalization includes a BMW X3 moving through an office, a scenario absent from the described training sources. Users can also traverse deserts, grasslands, water, and urban scenes. These demonstrations support the potential of combining game supervision with real footage to generate long, controllable visual experiences in settings with limited movement data.
neurips-2025-the-matrix-infinite-horizon.tldr: The Matrix combines game supervision and real-world footage to generate long, controllable 720p video streams with reported zero-shot transfer to new scenarios.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning uses a small labeled dataset together with unlabeled examples, often assigning predicted labels to the latter. TRiCo organizes this process around three roles: two student classifiers, a teacher, and an adversarial generator. The students learn on frozen, complementary representations, allowing the framework to work with existing vision backbones.

The teacher uses validation feedback to adapt pseudo-label selection and balance losses. Selection relies on mutual information rather than confidence, aiming for a more robust measure of uncertainty arising from the model’s knowledge. Meanwhile, a non-parametric generator perturbs embeddings to reveal weaknesses near decision boundaries. A Stackelberg-game formulation makes the teacher the strategy leader and the students followers under those perturbations.

Experiments on CIFAR-10, SVHN, STL-10, and ImageNet report consistently state-of-the-art performance when labels are scarce. The framework remains architecture-agnostic and compatible with frozen backbones. Its contribution is the coordinated interaction among adaptive supervision, complementary student views, and difficult generated examples, addressing several sources of fragility in pseudo-label-based learning together.
neurips-2025-trico-triadic-game-theoreti.tldr: TRiCo coordinates a teacher, two students, and adversarial embedding perturbations to improve semi-supervised learning when labeled examples are scarce.

paragraphs: Differential Transformers have shown strong empirical performance, but the explanation for their benefits has remained unclear. Their architecture also requires large-scale training from scratch, making existing pretrained weights difficult to reuse. This paper investigates the mechanism and uses its findings to design an adaptation method for pretrained language models.

The analysis identifies three contributing factors: greater expressivity through negative attention, less redundancy among attention heads, and improved learning dynamics. DEX incorporates these advantages by reusing existing softmax attention scores and adding a lightweight differential operation to the output value matrix. This places the new operation around computations that pretrained attention already provides.

Evaluations report substantial improvements across diverse language-model benchmarks with minimal adaptation data, stated as less than 0.01%. DEX is described as lightweight during both training and inference. The findings connect a mechanistic account of differential attention to a practical reuse strategy: pretrained models can gain its identified advantages through a small adaptation, making the analysis useful for architecture modification as well as understanding.
neurips-2025-understanding-differential-.tldr: DEX adds a lightweight differential operation to pretrained attention, bringing reported benchmark gains informed by an analysis of differential Transformers.
